source.title: Asymptotics of Linear Regression with Linearly Dependent Data

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper studies the double-descent phenomenon for ridge regression with linearly dependent data, a new setting, and reports how the error peak changes with redundancy.
record.gate_note: The paper measures estimation error across the dimension-to-sample ratio and reports a dependence-related shift in the double-descent peak. The plotted values are not tabulated. Results cited from other work are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study derives and simulates the estimation-error curve of ridge regression against γ = d/n for dependent (redundant) covariates. It states that the double-descent peak appears and shifts with redundancy, which bears on V4 in a new data setting.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors show double descent persists for ridge regression with linearly dependent data. Dependence shifts the peak and the under-to-overparameterization transition, which they attribute to a change in effective samples. They also show the optimal ridge parameter σε²γ/α² is independent of the dependence structure. In the text this is a qualitative observation from one example, not a quantified result.
record.recipe_differences: The study analyzes asymptotic estimation error for ridge regression with dependent covariates, rather than testing deep-network test error with the original sources’ settings.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported peak location changes with the redundancy setting ω.

fits_no_version.finding: With ridge tuned to the optimum (λ⋆ = σε²γ/α²) at γ = 2, estimation error decreases as redundancy decreases. The optimal λ does not depend on the dependence structure (Figures 2–3, Theorem 8).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Optimal ridge regularization is invariant to the temporal dependence of samples, while error at the optimum grows with redundancy.

record.problems: The double-descent curves are plotted rather than tabulated, and Figure 4’s caption gives a fixed γ while also describing error as a function of γ. The simulations average 50 trials, but no error bars or other uncertainty estimates are stated.
record.rows_left_out: No other claim-relevant results were reported separately with a suitable outcome measure. Figures 2 and 3 concern error as a function of redundancy or regularization, not a reported double-descent curve.

untested.parts: Training time and epochs are not studied.
Only the ratio γ = d/n is varied. Increasing n at fixed d near the threshold is not reported separately.
Only ridge regression with a linear dependence structure is tested, not multiple model classes. The second descent and the peak location are stated in words, not quantified.
The authors attribute the peak shift to 'effective samples' but do not test whether one complexity measure predicts the peak across axes.
Noise level is not varied. Multiple peaks are not examined. The optimal-λ results (Figures 2–3) are at fixed γ, so they do not show whether the peak disappears.
Complexity is not recounted with an effective number of parameters.

record.verdict_notes: This is a theoretical random-matrix study with simulations. Its measure is parameter estimation error, not test error. Ridge-regression double descent with i.i.d. data is already known (Hastie et al.), so the contribution to V4 is the dependent-data setting. The peak shift relates to V5's effective-complexity idea but is not a test of it. Rows r1–r2 serve only to validate theory against simulation.

versions.untested_parts: Error over training epochs is not studied.
The study varies the dimension-to-sample ratio, but does not report increasing sample count near the interpolation threshold as the intervention.
The study tests ridge regression with dependent covariates, not a broad range of model classes.
It discusses effective samples in relation to the peak’s location, but does not test whether one effective-complexity measure predicts peak location across size, epochs, and sample axes.

The study derives an optimal ridge parameter and studies regularization, but does not test whether noise drives the peak, whether multiple peaks occur, or whether optimally tuned regularization eliminates the peak.
The study does not recount complexity using an effective number of parameters or test whether that turns the second descent into an ordinary U-shaped curve.
